overview:
Samoa lies in the middle of the South Pacific, roughly halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii. Two large volcanic islands, Savai'i and Upolu, hold almost everyone, with several small islands nearby. The land totals about 2,840 km², a little smaller than Luxembourg, and it is green, steep and edged with reef.

About 220,000 people live in Samoa, speaking Samoan and English. Apia, on the north coast of Upolu, is the capital and only real town, a line of shops, churches and a busy market along a curved harbor.

Samoa is a parliamentary republic whose system blends elected government with the authority of matai, the chiefs who head extended families. Nearly all land is held by families rather than sold, and village life, church and family duty shape daily routines. Samoa was the first Pacific island nation to gain independence in the modern era, in 1962.
landAndNature: Both main islands are built from volcanoes, and Savai'i's Mount Silisili reaches about 1,860 meters. Savai'i's last big eruption, between 1905 and 1911, poured lava across villages, and the lava field with a church buried to its windows is still there. Rainforest covers the highlands, waterfalls spill into pools, and blowholes at Alofaaga shoot seawater high into the air through lava tubes. The To Sua ocean trench on Upolu is a deep garden sinkhole filled with clear seawater, reached by a long ladder. Coral reefs ring the coasts, and the tooth-billed pigeon, or manumea, Samoa's national bird and the closest living relative of the extinct dodo, is now critically endangered.
peopleAndCulture: Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, guides life: respect for elders, service to family, and ceremony. Villages are built around a malae, an open green where meetings and cricket are played, with open-sided fale houses shaded by thatch or tin. Tatau, the traditional tattoo applied by hand with combs of bone and wood, covers a man from waist to knee and takes days of painful work; women wear the finer malu. Feasts are cooked in an umu, an above-ground oven of hot stones, with taro, breadfruit, palusami, coconut cream baked in taro leaves, and fish. Rugby is a passion, and Samoans play for national and overseas teams in numbers far beyond the country's size. The siva is a graceful dance of hands and story.
history: Polynesians settled Samoa about 3,000 years ago, and the islands became a center from which voyagers sailed to Tonga, Fiji and beyond. Powerful chiefly titles and long rivalries shaped its politics for centuries. European missionaries arrived in the 1830s and Christianity spread quickly. Germany, Britain and the United States competed for the islands, and in 1899 they were split: the west went to Germany, the east became American Samoa. New Zealand took the German part in 1914 and administered it for decades. In 1918 a ship from New Zealand brought influenza that killed about a fifth of the population. The nonviolent Mau movement pressed for self-rule, and Samoa became independent on January 1, 1962. In 2011 the country skipped December 30 entirely to move west across the international date line.
funFacts: Samoa jumped from December 29 to December 31 in 2011, deleting a whole day to be on the same side of the date line as Australia and New Zealand.
Traditional Samoan tattooing is done by hand with bone combs and takes many painful days to complete.
Author Robert Louis Stevenson spent his last years in Samoa and is buried on a hilltop above Apia.
Samoa switched from driving on the right to driving on the left in 2009, one of very few countries ever to change sides.
Samoan cricket, kilikiti, uses a three-sided bat and can involve entire villages on the field at once.
